guide.p: Fluency is not speed. It means speaking at a natural pace, without long silences or constant self-correction, and linking your ideas so the listener can follow. A calm speaker who keeps going is more fluent than a fast speaker who keeps stopping.

bullets: Use natural fillers sparingly instead of silence: 'Well…', 'Let me think…', 'That's a good question…', 'What I mean is…'. Avoid repeating 'umm' or 'like'.
Don't stop to correct every small error. Fix it only if it changes the meaning, and do it quickly.
Use discourse markers to connect ideas: actually, on the other hand, the thing is, as a result, so.
If you can't find a word, describe it: 'the thing you use to…', 'a kind of…'. This is a skill examiners reward.
Practise speaking for two minutes on random topics every day, recording yourself.
Individual sounds — clear enough that words are not confused (ship/sheep, light/right, very/berry).
Word stress — PHOtograph, phoTOGraphy, photoGRAPHic. Wrong stress can make a word hard to recognise.
Sentence stress — the important words are stressed: 'I went to the MARKET, not the SUPERmarket.'
Connected speech — natural linking: 'an apple' → 'a-napple', 'want to' → 'wanna' in relaxed speech.
Intonation — rising and falling pitch to show questions, lists, surprise or contrast.
Chunking — pausing between groups of words, not in the middle of them.

guide.tip: Your accent does not matter. A strong accent that is easy to understand can score Band 8 or 9. What matters is clarity and control of these features.

bullets: Shadowing: play a short clip of a clear speaker, pause after each sentence and repeat it, copying the rhythm and stress.
Record your Part 2 answers and listen back. Mark where you paused too long or where a word was unclear.
Learn new words with their stress: write them with the stressed syllable in capitals (enVIRonment, ecoNOMic).
Read a paragraph aloud and mark the chunks with a slash before you read: 'In my opinion / the government should / invest more / in public transport.'
Speak to the examiner as you would to a friendly stranger — not too fast, not too quiet.
Ask for a repeat if you need it: 'Sorry, could you say that again?' This is not penalised.
Do not ask the examiner what a whole question means in Part 1, but in Part 3 you may ask them to rephrase.
